Usage

μ-law companding (compand = compress + expand). a is μ; b is the bit count.

It stretches the shadows with F(x) = ln(1 + mu*x) / ln(1 + mu), then quantizes, and returns via the inverse transform. As a result the steps become fine in the shadows and coarse in the highlights — since both the eye and the imaging system are sensitive to differences in the shadows, the visible degradation is smaller at the same bit count. It is the same principle as telephone speech coding (G.711); for images it amounts to a logarithmic allocation of grey levels.

a gives mu = 1 + 254*a (1-255; a=0 leaves it essentially unchanged), b is the bit count 1-8.

Difference from Lloyd–Max: that op fits the distribution of that image, so the code table changes from image to image. This op uses a fixed curve, so values can be compared as they are with other images and other devices. If the assumption that the distribution is logarithmically skewed holds, it performs similarly; if it does not, Lloyd–Max is better.

Conditions of use (with measurements): when the input is in [0,1] and pixels concentrate near 0. Compared with uniform quantization on synthetic images with an exponential distribution, concentration in the shadows lowers the squared error to 0.57 times (3 bit) and 0.51 times (5 bit). Concentration in the highlights instead makes it worse by 7.7 times (3 bit) and 18 times (5 bit) — an inspection image of dark scratches on a white background is exactly this case, so in that situation pass it through 1 - x before applying it. With very few levels (2 bit) the curve is too strong and it loses to uniform quantization even on a skewed distribution (measured 1.17 times).
